narration.text: You're standing above the Big Sioux River. The water ahead of you drops over Middle Sioux Falls, and Upper Sioux Falls is further upstream to your right. The full story of how these falls formed is still being researched and checked, and it will be added here once it is.

stops.name: The river and the Dakota
stops.placement: provisional: an OpenStreetMap viewpoint node on the path; confirm on site with Parks staff

facing.hint: Face upstream, toward the upper falls

narration.text: People were coming to this river long before there was a city here. Use of this place by Indigenous people goes back thousands of years, as a hub for trade and seasonal travel. A historical marker in this park, put up in 2025, describes the Dakota, one of the three prominent subcultures of the Oceti Sakowin people, using the river and the falls as a trading and reference point.

stops.name: The Queen Bee Mill
stops.placement: provisional: an OpenStreetMap information-board node near the mill; confirm on site with Parks staff

narration.text: What's left in front of you is the Queen Bee Mill. Richard Pettigrew built it in 1881, and it closed in 1883, only two years later. The land at the falls had been fought over even before that: in 1856, the Western Town Company and the Dakota Land Company competed to claim the site.
